q: Which of these is a common purpose of a website?
why: Websites commonly exist for eCommerce, to provide information, to promote products/services, or for entertainment â€” all are valid purposes.

q: What is a user persona?
options: A fictional profile representing a typical user
A type of website security test
why: A user persona is a made-up but realistic profile of a typical user â€” their age, goals, habits and frustrations â€” used to design for real people.

q: Which reading pattern do users most commonly follow on text-heavy websites?
why: Eye-tracking shows users scan in an F-shape: horizontal lines across the top, then down the left edge. Put key info where eyes go first.

q: Which layout pattern is best suited to a simple homepage with a strong headline and a call to action?
why: The Z-pattern suits hero pages: the eye moves top-left, then top-right, then diagonally to the bottom-right where the call to action sits.

q: What is a benefit of a fixed/sticky navigation bar?
options: It makes the page load faster
Navigation is always visible while scrolling
It removes the need for a sitemap
why: A sticky nav stays visible as the user scrolls, so they can always find their way around without scrolling back to the top.

q: Which describes 'visual hierarchy' in page design?
options: Placing elements in order of importance so users notice key things first
Making every element the same size
why: Visual hierarchy uses size, colour, spacing and position to guide the eye from the most to the least important content.

q: Why is sufficient colour contrast between text and background important?
options: It makes the site look more colourful
It helps users with visual impairments read the content
It is only for aesthetic appeal
why: Good contrast (WCAG recommends at least 4.5:1 for normal text) makes text readable for everyone, including users with low vision.

q: Which of these is an accessibility feature?
why: Accessibility includes keyboard navigation, alt text, transcripts and captions, breadcrumbs, customisable features and more.

q: What is a micro-interaction?
options: A short feedback animation, like a button changing colour when clicked
why: Micro-interactions are small animations that give feedback â€” like a button press effect. Every use of motion should have a purpose.

q: What makes a website 'dynamic'?
options: It customises the user experience or controls access to content, often using server-side processing
It changes colours automatically each day
why: Dynamic sites serve customised experiences (recommendations, member areas) â€” usually powered by a server and database, not fixed static pages.

q: Why must a website be tested across different browsers and devices?
options: Because browsers render HTML, CSS and JS with slight differences
It is a legal requirement in the UK
To increase the number of users
why: Browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge) and devices (phone, tablet, desktop) can render the same code slightly differently, so cross-browser testing catches discrepancies.

q: Which of these helps with search engine optimisation (SEO)?
options: Using descriptive page titles and meta descriptions
Using only images (no text) on the page
Hiding keywords in the page background
why: SEO uses keywords, descriptive titles, meta descriptions, headings, alt text and fast, mobile-friendly pages to help search engines rank your site.

q: Which of these should you establish first when planning from a client brief?
options: The client's requirements: purpose, audience and technical needs
why: Everything else â€” structure, design, content â€” flows from understanding the purpose, the intended audience and the technical requirements of the brief.

q: You find a great photo on Google Images for your client's website. What should you do?
options: Use it â€” everything online is free to use
Check the licence and credit the source, or use royalty-free images
Crop it so the owner won't recognise it
Only use it if the site is not making money
why: Most images are protected by copyright. Check the licence, credit the source, use Creative Commons or royalty-free stock, or create your own assets.

q: Your site has a form where users enter their email. Under UK GDPR, what must you provide?
options: A privacy policy explaining what you collect and why, plus consent
Nothing â€” small sites are exempt
why: GDPR applies to any site processing personal data. You must be transparent about what data you collect, why, and get consent where needed.

q: What is a wireframe?
options: The final finished design with colours and images
A low-fidelity layout of a page showing the structure and placement of elements
why: Wireframes are simple boxes and placeholders showing where elements go â€” structure first, style later.

q: Which is a wireframing tool or technique?
why: Wireframes can be sketched on paper, drawn in graphic design software, built in UX tools like Figma, or made in dedicated apps.

q: Which file format is usually best for a photographic image on a website?
why: JPG compresses photographs well. PNG suits graphics with transparency, SVG suits logos and icons, MP4 is for video.

q: Why compress and resize images before adding them to a website?
options: Large files slow the page down, hurting user experience and SEO
Because the HTML standard requires it
why: Large images increase loading time, which frustrates users (especially on mobile) and hurts search ranking. Compress to the size you actually use.

q: What is good practice for naming asset files?
options: Use consistent, descriptive names with no spaces (e.g. hero-banner.jpg)
Use the person who downloaded it as the name
Use random characters so they cannot clash
why: Descriptive names with dashes (hero-banner.jpg) are readable, consistent and don't break URLs â€” unlike 'IMG 3421.JPG'.

q: What is an asset log used for?
options: Tracking each asset â€” its name, source and where it appears on the site
why: An asset log shows where each asset came from (original work vs sourced, with credit) and how it's used â€” great evidence for the assignment.

q: Which HTML element is semantic (has meaning for accessibility and SEO)?
why: Semantic elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section> and <footer> describe their meaning, helping screen readers and search engines.

q: Which describes the CSS box model?
why: Every element is a box: content in the middle, then padding (space inside), border, and margin (space outside).

q: How do you make a layout responsive to different screen sizes?
options: Media queries and responsive layout tools like Flexbox and Grid
why: Media queries apply different styles at different screen widths, and Flexbox/Grid layouts flex to fit. Never rely on fixed widths alone.

q: Which JavaScript-powered component reveals and hides content in a collapsible section?
why: An accordion lets users expand and collapse sections â€” great for FAQs. Modals overlay the page; carousels slide images.

q: What does a modal box do?
options: Opens an overlay on top of the page (e.g. an enlarged image or a sign-in dialog)
why: A modal displays content in an overlay. Clicking a thumbnail to view a larger image in a modal is a common assignment requirement.

q: Which organisation publishes the WCAG accessibility guidelines?
why: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) publishes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).

q: What is the purpose of alt text on an image?
options: Describes the image for screen readers and shows if the image fails to load
Adds a border around the image
why: Alt text gives a text description of the image for screen readers and appears when the image can't load.

q: Which of these would you check during functionality testing?
options: Whether users find the site intuitive
Whether the brand name is memorable
why: Functionality testing checks that things WORK â€” links, buttons, forms, interactions and responsiveness. Usability testing checks how real users experience the site.

q: What is usability testing?
options: Asking real users to try the site and give feedback on navigation, clarity and experience
Running the site through a code validator
Checking the site loads on one computer
why: Usability testing uses real users (classmates, friends, family) to audit the experience â€” accessibility, logical navigation, clarity and overall UX.

q: What is a test plan?
options: A table of tests listing description, test data, expected outcome, actual outcome and comments
A schedule of when to write code
A wireframe of the final site
why: A formal test plan documents each test so you can compare expected vs actual outcomes â€” essential evidence for the assignment.

q: What should your self-review of the finished website consider?
options: Quality vs similar sites, suitability for the audience, meeting client requirements, consistency and readability
why: The spec's self-review covers comparison with similar websites, audience and purpose suitability, client requirements, legal/ethical constraints, consistency and readability.

q: Which of these is an example of an entertainment website?
options: A streaming service showing films and series
why: Entertainment sites exist to amuse or engage users â€” streaming, gaming, music and video platforms are classic examples.

q: What is the main purpose of an eCommerce website?
options: To sell products or services online
To display a company's contact details only
why: eCommerce sites are built to sell â€” they include product listings, a shopping basket, checkout and payment processing.

q: Why is it important to identify the target audience before designing a website?
options: So the design, content and tone match what the audience expects
Because all websites must have an audience
To set the price of the website
why: Knowing the audience (age, interests, technical ability) shapes everything â€” layout, colour, language, features and content.

q: Which of these is a demographic factor used to define a target audience?
why: Demographics include age, gender, income, education, location and occupation â€” all used to build a picture of the audience.

q: What is the purpose of grouping related content together on a page?
options: To make the page easier to scan and understand
To make the page load faster
To reduce the number of images
why: Grouping related items (e.g. all navigation together, all product cards together) helps users find what they need quickly.

q: What is a grid layout in web design?
options: A system of columns and rows used to align content consistently
why: A grid divides the page into columns and rows so elements align neatly â€” the basis of most professional layouts.

q: What is a hamburger menu?
options: A navigation icon (three lines) that expands a menu, common on mobile
why: The hamburger icon (â˜°) collapses navigation into a button, saving space on small screens â€” a common responsive pattern.

q: What is logical navigation?
options: Organising pages in a way that makes sense to the user, matching how they think
why: Logical navigation groups pages by meaning (e.g. all 'About' pages together) so users can predict where to find things.

q: What is a call to action (CTA)?
options: A button or link that prompts the user to take a specific action, like 'Buy now'
why: A CTA guides the user toward a goal â€” 'Sign up', 'Buy now', 'Contact us' â€” and should be visually prominent.

q: Why is typography important in web design?
options: It affects readability and the overall feel of the site
why: Font choice, size, spacing and weight affect how easily users read and how professional the site looks.

q: What is a colour scheme?
options: The set of colours used consistently across a website
why: A colour scheme is a deliberate palette used for backgrounds, text, buttons and accents to create a consistent brand feel.

q: What does 'consistency' mean in user experience design?
options: Using the same layout, colours and patterns throughout the site
why: Consistency means users learn how the site works once and can apply it everywhere â€” reducing confusion and frustration.

q: Why should a website be 'user-friendly'?
options: So users can achieve their goals easily without frustration
Because it is a legal requirement
To make it harder to use
why: A user-friendly site is intuitive, fast and accessible, so visitors stay longer and are more likely to return or convert.

q: Why should motion on a website be used sparingly?
options: Too much motion distracts users and can hurt accessibility and performance
why: Motion should have a purpose (feedback, guidance). Excessive animation distracts, slows the page and can trigger accessibility issues.

q: Which of these is an example of dynamic content?
why: Dynamic content changes based on the user or data â€” recommendations, member dashboards, live scores and search results.

q: What is cross-browser compatibility?
options: A website working correctly across different browsers
A site that only works in one browser
why: Cross-browser compatibility means the site renders and functions correctly in Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge and others.

q: What is a meta description?
options: A short summary of a page shown in search results
why: A meta description is a brief snippet that appears under the page title in search results, helping users decide whether to click.

q: Why is a mobile-friendly (responsive) website important for SEO?
options: Google prioritises mobile-friendly sites in search rankings
It reduces the number of pages
why: Google uses mobile-first indexing, so a responsive site ranks better and provides a better experience for mobile users.

q: What is a client brief?
options: A document describing what the client wants the website to achieve
A type of contract for hosting
why: The brief sets out the purpose, audience, features, tone and constraints â€” the starting point for all planning.

q: Which of these is a technical requirement you might establish from a brief?
why: Technical requirements include hosting, domain, platform, performance, security and compatibility needs.

q: Why research existing websites before designing a new one?
options: To learn what works well and what to avoid
why: Researching similar sites reveals best practice, common features and gaps you can improve on â€” evidence for the assignment.

q: What is copyright?
options: The legal right of the creator to control how their work is used
why: Copyright protects original work (text, images, music, code). You need permission or a licence to use someone else's work.

q: What is a Creative Commons licence?
options: A licence that lets creators share their work with certain conditions
why: Creative Commons licences allow reuse under set conditions (e.g. attribution, non-commercial) â€” a safe source of assets.

q: Why must a website be accessible to users with disabilities?
options: It is a legal requirement under the Equality Act and improves the experience for everyone
why: The Equality Act 2010 requires websites to be accessible, and accessibility also benefits all users (e.g. captions, keyboard nav).

q: What is the difference between a wireframe and a mockup?
options: A wireframe is low-fidelity structure; a mockup is a high-fidelity visual design
A mockup is a wireframe with no text
A wireframe is the final code
why: Wireframes show structure and layout in simple boxes; mockups add colour, images and typography to show the final look.

q: Why annotate a wireframe?
options: To explain the purpose of each element and how it meets the brief
why: Annotations show your thinking â€” why each element is there and how it meets client requirements â€” key evidence for the assignment.

q: What is a visual style?
options: The consistent look created by colour palette, typography, imagery and layout
why: The visual style ties together colour, fonts, images and spacing to create a cohesive, recognisable brand.

q: What is a brand identity?
options: The visual and verbal elements that represent a company (logo, colours, tone)
why: Brand identity includes the logo, colour palette, typography and tone of voice that make a company recognisable.

q: What does 'fitness for purpose' mean when reviewing a design?
options: Whether the design meets the client's requirements and works for the audience
why: Fitness for purpose asks: does this design actually do what the client and audience need? Review it against the brief.

q: Which file format is best for a logo with a transparent background?
why: PNG supports transparency, so a logo can sit on any background. SVG is even better for logos as it scales without losing quality.

q: What is a vector graphic?
options: An image made of paths that scales without losing quality (e.g. SVG)
why: Vector graphics use mathematical paths, so they stay sharp at any size â€” ideal for logos, icons and diagrams.

q: Why trim a video before adding it to a website?
options: To remove unnecessary footage and reduce file size
why: Trimming removes unwanted parts, reducing file size and loading time while keeping the content focused.

q: What is a folder structure for assets?
options: An organised set of folders (e.g. images/, css/, js/) to keep files tidy
why: A clear folder structure makes assets easy to find, maintain and reference â€” good practice and good evidence.

q: What is the difference between original and sourced assets?
options: Original assets you create yourself; sourced assets you obtain from elsewhere (with credit)
Original assets are free; sourced are paid
why: Creating your own assets shows skill; sourcing others requires credit and licence checks. Both are valid if managed properly.

q: Which HTML tag is used to create a hyperlink?
why: The (anchor) tag creates links using the href attribute, e.g. Link.

q: Which HTML element is used for a form?
why: The <form> element wraps form controls like inputs, selects and buttons, and defines how data is submitted.

q: Which HTML tag embeds a video?
why: The <video> element embeds video with controls, e.g. <video controls src="clip.mp4"></video>.

q: What is the purpose of the <nav> element?
options: To mark up a block of navigation links
why: <nav> is a semantic element that identifies navigation links, helping screen readers and SEO understand the structure.

q: What does CSS stand for?
why: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the presentation â€” layout, colours, fonts and spacing â€” of HTML content.

q: Which CSS property changes the text colour?
why: The color property sets text colour; background sets the background; font-size sets size; text-align aligns text.

q: What is a media query used for?
options: Applying different styles based on screen size or device
why: Media queries (e.g. @media (max-width: 600px)) apply CSS only under certain conditions â€” the basis of responsive design.

q: What is Flexbox used for?
options: Laying out elements in a flexible row or column
why: Flexbox arranges items in one dimension (row or column) and handles spacing, alignment and wrapping â€” great for nav bars and cards.

q: What is JavaScript used for on a website?
options: Adding interactivity like sliders, forms and dynamic content
why: JavaScript adds behaviour and interactivity â€” responding to clicks, validating forms, animating and updating content.

q: What does a carousel/slider do?
options: Cycles through a set of images or slides
why: A carousel automatically or manually cycles through slides â€” common for galleries, testimonials and featured content.

q: What is a tab component?
options: A set of buttons that switch between different content panels
why: Tabs let users switch between sections of content without leaving the page â€” a common interactive component.

q: What is a filter/search feature?
options: Lets users narrow down a list by typing or selecting criteria
why: Search/filter functionality lets users find items quickly â€” a common assignment requirement (e.g. filtering a product list).

q: What is a skip link?
options: A link that lets keyboard users jump straight to the main content
why: A skip link ('Skip to main content') lets keyboard and screen-reader users bypass repeated navigation â€” an accessibility best practice.

q: What is semantic HTML?
options: Using elements that describe their meaning (e.g. <header>, <main>)
HTML that only works in one browser
why: Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags, improving accessibility, SEO and code readability compared to generic <div>s.

q: Why is the lang attribute important on the <html> element?
options: It tells screen readers and search engines the page language
why: The lang attribute (e.g. lang="en") helps screen readers pronounce content correctly and helps search engines index the language.

q: What is a heading hierarchy?
options: Using h1, h2, h3 in a logical order to structure content
why: A logical heading hierarchy (one h1, then h2/h3 for subsections) helps screen readers and search engines understand structure.

q: What is a sitemap in the context of SEO?
options: A file listing all pages of a site to help search engines index it
why: An XML sitemap lists all URLs so search engines can discover and index pages efficiently.

q: What is a test plan's 'expected outcome'?
options: What the site should do if the feature works correctly
why: The expected outcome is the correct result you predict; comparing it to the actual outcome reveals whether the feature works.

q: What is a test plan's 'actual outcome'?
options: What the site actually did when tested
why: The actual outcome records what really happened, so you can compare it to the expected outcome and note any defects.

q: What is a defect/bug?
options: An error or fault in the website that stops it working as intended
why: A defect is any flaw â€” a broken link, a form that won't submit, a layout that breaks on mobile â€” that needs fixing.

q: Why test a website on a mobile device?
options: To check the responsive layout works and content is usable on small screens
why: Most users browse on mobile, so you must verify the responsive layout, touch targets and readability on small screens.

q: What is a usability audit?
options: A structured review of how easy and pleasant the site is to use
why: A usability audit assesses navigation, clarity, accessibility and overall user experience â€” often with real users.

q: What is a refinement?
options: A change made to improve the website after testing or review
why: Refinements are improvements made in response to testing and feedback â€” showing the review cycle is key evidence.

q: Why document the improvements you made after testing?
options: To show the examiner you reviewed and refined your work
Because it is required by law
why: Documenting before â†’ feedback â†’ after shows the review cycle, which is essential for higher grades in the assignment.

q: Which of these is a purpose of a promotional website?
options: To advertise a product or service and encourage action
why: Promotional sites market a product/service, using CTAs and persuasive content to drive sales or enquiries.

q: What is an informational website?
options: A site whose main purpose is to provide facts and details
why: Informational sites (news, encyclopaedias, company 'about' pages) exist to deliver facts and knowledge.

q: What is a user journey?
options: The path a user takes through a website to reach a goal
why: A user journey maps the steps a visitor takes â€” from landing to completing a task â€” helping you spot friction points.

q: What is whitespace (negative space) in design?
options: The empty space between elements that improves readability and focus
why: Whitespace gives content room to breathe, making layouts cleaner and easier to scan â€” a key design principle.

q: What is a breadcrumb?
options: A navigation trail showing the user's location in the site hierarchy
why: Breadcrumbs (e.g. Home â€º Products â€º Laptops) show where you are and let users jump back up the hierarchy.

q: What is a hero section?
options: The large prominent area at the top of a homepage with the main headline and CTA
why: The hero is the first thing users see â€” a big headline, supporting text and a call to action that sets the tone.

q: What is a logo?
options: A symbol or design that identifies a brand
why: A logo is a recognisable mark that represents a company â€” a key part of brand identity.

q: What is a loading time and why does it matter?
options: How long a page takes to load; slow pages frustrate users and hurt SEO
why: Fast loading improves user experience and search ranking; slow sites lose visitors. Optimise images and code.

q: What is a static website?
options: A site with fixed content that doesn't change based on the user
why: Static sites serve the same content to everyone (e.g. a simple brochure site) â€” simpler but less personalised.

q: What is a keyword?
options: A word or phrase users type into a search engine
why: Keywords are the terms people search for; using them naturally in titles, headings and content helps SEO.

q: What is a constraint in a client brief?
options: A limitation or requirement the design must work within (e.g. budget, deadline, brand rules)
why: Constraints are boundaries â€” budget, time, brand colours, accessibility, legal rules â€” that shape the design.

q: What is a competitor analysis?
options: Reviewing similar websites to see what they do well and poorly
why: Analysing competitors reveals best practice, gaps and opportunities â€” strong evidence for the planning task.

q: What is a privacy policy?
options: A statement explaining what personal data a site collects and how it's used
why: A privacy policy is required under GDPR to be transparent about data collection, use and user rights.

q: What is GDPR?
options: The General Data Protection Regulation governing personal data
why: GDPR is EU/UK law protecting personal data â€” sites must be transparent, get consent and protect user data.

q: What is a low-fidelity wireframe?
options: A rough, simple sketch showing basic structure without detail
why: Low-fidelity wireframes are quick, rough sketches (often on paper) to explore layout before investing in detail.

q: What is a high-fidelity mockup?
options: A detailed, polished design showing colours, fonts and images
why: High-fidelity mockups look close to the final site, showing the visual style in detail before coding.

q: What is a design review?
options: Assessing the design against the brief and audience to identify improvements
why: A design review compares the design to the brief and audience needs, identifying what to improve â€” key for the assignment.

q: What is image compression?
options: Reducing an image's file size while keeping acceptable quality
why: Compression reduces file size (faster loading) with minimal quality loss â€” essential for web performance.

q: What is a royalty-free image?
options: An image you can use without paying ongoing royalties, usually with a licence
An image that is always free with no conditions
why: Royalty-free means you pay once (or it's free) and can use it, but you should still check the licence terms.

q: Which HTML element is used for a table?
why: The <table> element creates tables, with <tr> for rows, <th> for headers and <td> for cells.

q: What is the purpose of the CSS 'margin' property?
options: To add space outside an element, pushing it away from neighbours
To add space inside an element
why: Margin adds space outside the border; padding adds space inside. Both control spacing in the box model.

q: What is an event listener in JavaScript?
options: Code that waits for an action (like a click) and runs a function in response
why: Event listeners (e.g. addEventListener('click', ...)) make elements interactive by responding to user actions.
